common_name: Pride of Summerville Azalea (Deep Rose-Pink Charleston-Area Heirloom)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Pride of Summerville is a Southern Indica azalea associated with the historic azalea gardens around Summerville and Charleston, South Carolina.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade, allowing plenty of room for the mature shrub's spread. Pride of Summerville is a historic Southern Indica azalea long associated with the famed heirloom azalea gardens around Summerville and Charleston, South Carolina, prized for its deep, rich rose-pink flowers produced in an overwhelming spring flush on a large, vigorous evergreen shrub. Like other Southern Indica cultivars it provides substantial year-round structure and a spectacular seasonal display, making it a strong choice for large borders, screens, and historic garden restorations. Water deeply during establishment and dry periods, and prune only right after flowering if shaping is needed, since next year's flower buds form soon after bloom ends.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Azaleas for Texas Gardens

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kirin is one of the original 50 Kurume azalea selections introduced to the West by plant collector E.H. Wilson in 1918.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation. Kirin is one of E.H. Wilson's original fifty Kurume azalea introductions brought from Japan to the West in 1918, a historic selection still valued for its dense, rounded habit and abundant deep pink, hose-in-hose flowers that cover the shrub in a heavy spring flush. Its long history and reliable performance have kept it in circulation among azalea collectors and Southern gardens for over a century. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Azaleas for Texas Gardens

common_name: Ward's Ruby Azalea (Compact Dark Red Kurume Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ward's Ruby is a slow-growing, compact Kurume azalea valued for its very dark red flowers and good cold hardiness to zone 8.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation. Ward's Ruby is a slow-growing, compact Kurume azalea bearing very dark, saturated red flowers in a dense spring flush, its small mature size making it especially useful for foundation plantings, rock gardens, and smaller borders where larger Southern Indica cultivars would not fit. Its good cold hardiness and manageable size have kept it a reliable, long-favored selection among compact red azaleas. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Azaleas for Texas Gardens

common_name: Sherwood Red Azalea (Compact Bright Red Kurume-Type Azalea)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in spring or fall in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Sherwood Red is a compact, semi-dwarf Kurume-type azalea bred for a dense habit and bright red spring bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 4.5-6.0), humus-rich soil in partial shade with good air circulation. Sherwood Red is a compact, semi-dwarf Kurume-type azalea prized for its bright, clear red flowers produced in a dense spring flush on a tidy, well-branched shrub that fits easily into foundation plantings, borders, and mass plantings without regular pruning. Its smaller mature size compared to Southern Indica cultivars makes it a practical choice where space is limited but a vivid red spring display is still wanted. Water deeply during dry spells, especially while establishing, and prune lightly right after flowering if shaping is needed, since flower buds for next year's bloom set soon after the spring flush ends.
sources: University of Georgia Cooperative Extension — Azalea Cultivars for the Landscape
Texas A&M AgriLife Extension — Azaleas for Texas Gardens

common_name: Betty Sheffield Camellia (Iconic White Picotee-Edged Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Betty Sheffield is one of the most iconic Southern camellia families, known for its large white flowers streaked and edged in red or pink.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Betty Sheffield is one of the most celebrated Camellia japonica cultivars in Southern gardening, producing huge, formal to semi-double blooms in white edged and streaked with red or pink in an ever-varying, unpredictable picotee pattern that has made it a favorite exhibition flower for generations. The large, upright, vigorous evergreen shrub blooms in mid to late winter and provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its dramatic flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Grand Slam Camellia (Bright Red Peony-Form Camellia japonica)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Grand Slam is a popular award-winning Camellia japonica cultivar valued for its large, vivid red, semi-double to peony-form flowers.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun. Grand Slam is a widely grown Camellia japonica cultivar bearing large, bright, true red flowers in a loose semi-double to peony form packed with ruffled petals, one of the most vivid reds available among camellia cultivars and a longtime award winner on the camellia show circuit. The vigorous, upright evergreen shrub blooms in mid-season and provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its striking winter flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Kumasaka Camellia (Cold-Hardy Rose-Pink Japanese Heirloom Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Kumasaka is an old Japanese Camellia japonica cultivar noted for exceptional cold hardiness among japonica cultivars.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Kumasaka is a historic Japanese Camellia japonica cultivar producing rose-pink, rose-form double flowers with neatly overlapping petals, valued not only for its classic, elegant bloom form but for cold hardiness above average for the species, which has helped it remain in cultivation across a broader hardiness range than many other japonica cultivars. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub blooms in midseason and provides dense, glossy year-round structure. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

common_name: Ville de Nantes Camellia (Red-and-White Marbled French Heirloom Camellia)

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Ville de Nantes, introduced in France in 1910, bears distinctive red flowers marbled and streaked with white on loosely notched petals.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade with protection from harsh afternoon sun. Ville de Nantes, introduced in France in 1910, is a distinctive antique Camellia japonica cultivar bearing loose, peony-form red flowers irregularly marbled and streaked with white, the notched, informal petal edges giving each bloom a slightly ragged, old-fashioned character unlike the smoother forms of many other camellias. It blooms in mid to late season on an upright, vigorous evergreen shrub that provides dense, glossy year-round structure in addition to its unusual flowers. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.

planting.note: Plant container shrubs in fall or early spring in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade; Magnoliiflora, an 1888 Japanese heirloom, bears smaller, semi-double blush-pink flowers resembling a small magnolia bloom.

directions: Plant in moist, well-drained, acidic (pH 5.0-6.5), humus-rich soil in partial shade, with morning sun and afternoon shade to protect the glossy foliage from scorch. Magnoliiflora is an antique Camellia japonica cultivar dating to around 1888, named for its smaller, semi-double, soft blush-pink flowers whose loosely arranged petals and prominent stamens give them a delicate resemblance to a small magnolia bloom, a distinctive form among the many fuller, more formal camellia types. It flowers later in the season than many other japonica cultivars, extending camellia bloom into late winter and early spring. The upright, vigorous evergreen shrub provides dense, glossy year-round structure. Mulch heavily with pine bark or pine straw to maintain the acidic, evenly moist soil camellias need, and prune only to remove dead or crossing branches after bloom.
